messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq Mansour is a forty-year-old Lebanese-American software engineer who presents for an initial psychological evaluation approximately fourteen months after surviving a catastrophic tornado that struck the suburban Tennessee neighborhood where he lives with his wife. He reports a PCL-5 score of 37, consistent with clinically significant post-traumatic stress, and describes a life that has narrowed considerably since the storm.

The tornado made landfall on a Tuesday afternoon in early spring. Tariq was working from home, seated at his desk in the study, when the sky outside his window turned a color he later struggled to describe. The warning sirens had sounded only seconds before the structure began to shake. What followed was perhaps forty seconds of total sensory obliteration: the freight-train roar that seemed to come from inside the walls, the concussive pressure change that popped his ears, the sound of glass exploding inward, and then the particular crack of the roof separating from the house above him. He was thrown from his chair and found himself pinned beneath a collapsed bookcase as the storm passed. He lay there in silence broken only by settling debris and a distant car alarm, unable to fully reconstruct, even now, the exact sequence of what happened between the moment the sirens sounded and the moment he found himself on the floor. The memories arrive not as a coherent story but as fragments — the green light, the roar, a sensation of weightlessness, cold air on his face — and when they surface, they do not feel like recollections. They feel like the present moment. He can hear the crack of the roof as clearly as if he were still beneath it.

In the weeks after the storm, Tariq returned to remote work quickly, telling his wife and colleagues that staying busy was the healthiest thing he could do. He made a deliberate practice of redirecting his thoughts toward gratitude — the house was repairable, no one had died, he still had his job. He repeated these facts to himself with something close to discipline. What he could not explain, and did not share with anyone, was that this effort of positive redirection required nearly constant vigilance and left him exhausted by midday.

His work as a software engineer means he spends long hours at a standing desk in a rebuilt home office, and it is here that the physical residue of the tornado is most present. A colleague joining a video call and leaning suddenly toward the camera, a coworker's hand landing on his shoulder during an in-person sprint review at the office — these moments produce a sharp, full-body alarm response that he finds deeply embarrassing. He has begun positioning himself near the exit in conference rooms before any meeting begins, scanning the layout before he can settle. He tells himself this is practical. What frightens him most is the private conviction that he would not be fast enough if something happened again, and that this is, in some fundamental way, his own fault. Someone more capable, he has come to believe, would not have been caught unprepared in their own home.

He has not been to a doctor since the storm, canceling two follow-up appointments for a minor hand laceration he sustained that day. The sight of an ambulance on the highway causes him to change lanes and, if possible, take an alternate route. He cannot fully articulate why, only that proximity to medical settings feels like an acknowledgment he is not ready to make.

His wife has noticed that he is different — quieter, quicker to irritate, and absent in a way she cannot name. He knows she has noticed. He finds himself spending long mental hours rehearsing grievances toward the local emergency management system, turning over questions of negligence and accountability that have no practical outlet. He is aware these thoughts are unproductive. He cannot stop them.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a conversation with his wife in which she told him, gently, that she missed him. He had no answer for her. He had come to believe, with a quiet certainty that frightened him, that the person she missed was simply gone — that happiness was something that had belonged to a previous version of himself and that nothing waiting ahead of him would restore it. He arrives at intake hoping, with some ambivalence, to be proven wrong.
